name: wafw00f – WAF Detection
description: Detect and fingerprint Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) by sending crafted HTTP requests and analysing responses. Knowing the WAF vendor helps select appropriate bypass techniques before launching attacks.
notes: wafw00f fingerprints by looking at HTTP response headers, cookies (e.g. __cfduid for Cloudflare), and response body differences when sending malicious payloads. Use -a to test all known WAFs (slower but thorough). Install via pip3 if not present. WAF detection should happen before fuzzing or injection attempts so you can tune payloads accordingly.

variations.caption: Test against all known WAF signatures (thorough)
variations.label: wafw00f https://<target> -a

variations.caption: Verbose output — shows each probe and response
variations.label: wafw00f https://<target> -v

examples.caption: CWES M04: detect WAF before launching web attacks on target

source: CWES Module 04: Information Gathering - Web Edition

recommended.note: Follow WAF detection with nikto fingerprinting scan
FinalRecon runs multiple recon tasks including WAF-like header analysis

defense.why_it_works: wafw00f sends crafted requests and analyses the responses (headers, cookies, block pages, status codes) to fingerprint the WAF vendor and product sitting in front of a site — so the tester knows what protection exists before probing further.
defense.prerequisites: Network access to the target web application (URL).
defense.impact: Identification of the WAF vendor/product (e.g. Wordfence) protecting the target, which informs the evasion techniques needed in subsequent testing and avoids false negatives.
defense.detection:
Low to Moderate: wafw00f sends a small set of crafted probe requests. A WAF can block, alter, or log these fingerprinting attempts and may alert — the probes are few but distinctive, and a WAF is designed to notice anomalous requests.

[MITRE T1595.002] The active, crafted-request pattern is loggable at the WAF and web server.
defense.artifacts: A handful of crafted/anomalous probe requests in web and WAF logs; WAF detection events for the fingerprinting payloads.
defense.prevention:
Configure the WAF to return generic responses that do not reveal its vendor identity (uniform block pages, no vendor-specific headers or cookies); monitor WAF logs for fingerprinting probe patterns and known scanner signatures.

[MITRE T1595.002 M1056] Minimise identifying information exposed to external parties.
defense.evasion: Only a few crafted requests are sent, so low-and-slow timing and a benign user-agent reduce the footprint — though a well-tuned WAF may still log the probes.
defense.misconfiguration: Services expose excessive information: version banners, supported auth methods, valid usernames via error responses. IPMI has no authentication (version 2.0 cipher 0 vulnerability). RSH/rexec trust .rhosts files. rsync shares readable anonymously. Oracle TNS allows remote poisoning in older versions.
defense.vulnerable_config:
# IPMI cipher 0 — no authentication required:
# ipmitool -H <ip> -U admin -P '' -I lanplus -C 0 chassis status
# Returns valid data — auth bypassed entirely

# rsync anonymous access:
# rsync --list-only rsync://<ip>/  # lists all modules without auth
# rsync rsync://<ip>/backup /tmp   # downloads backup files

# Oracle TNS — version banner reveals exact version:
# nmap -p 1521 -sV -> Oracle Database 11.2.0.4 (exact version)
defense.secure_config:
# IPMI — disable cipher 0, enable only strong ciphers:
# /etc/ipmi/ipmievd.conf: IPMI_CIPHER_SUITE=17  (AES, mandatory auth)
# Or disable IPMI entirely if not needed (BMC IPMI = critical attack surface)

# rsync — require auth:
# /etc/rsyncd.conf:
# [backup]
#   auth users = backupuser
#   secrets file = /etc/rsyncd.secrets
#   hosts allow = 10.10.1.0/24

# RSH/rexec — disable entirely (replaced by SSH):
systemctl disable rsh.socket rexec.socket rlogin.socket

# Oracle TNS — disable remote admin, enforce auth:
# sqlnet.ora: SQLNET.AUTHENTICATION_SERVICES = (BEQ, TCPS)  (not NONE)
